records.sourceFile: Lower Limb Joint Mechanics during Maximal Accelerative and Decelerative Running.pdf

paper.citation: Fitzwilliam E, Steventon-Lorenzen N, Opar D, Schache AG, Maniar N. Lower Limb Joint Mechanics during Maximal Accelerative and Decelerative Running. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2024. Published ahead of print.
paper.abstract: This laboratory study compared hip, knee and ankle joint moments and work in 20 recreationally active adults performing maximal-effort accelerations and unanticipated decelerations. Net joint work was positive during acceleration and negative during deceleration, with the ankle contributing most positive work in acceleration and the knee and hip contributing most negative work in deceleration. Peak joint moments were generally larger during deceleration, except for the ankle plantarflexion and hip flexion moments.
paper.tldr: In recreationally active adults, maximal acceleration relied mainly on positive work from the ankle and hip, while deceleration relied on negative work from the knee and hip. Peak moments were generally greater in deceleration, which may inform training, but the study measured mechanics rather than performance or injury.
paper.methods: Laboratory study. Twenty recreationally active adults (10 men, 10 women; age 25 +/- 4 years; mass 70 +/- 10 kg; at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week) performed three maximal acceleration trials and three deceleration trials, in which a light at a second timing gate randomly signalled stop or continue. Marker-based motion capture, two force plates and OpenSim inverse dynamics with a 31 degree-of-freedom model gave hip, knee and ankle moments, power and work. Linear mixed models with participant as a random effect were used, with p < 0.01 as the significance threshold; 118 of 120 trials were analysed after two non-decelerative trials were excluded.
paper.findings: Net joint work was positive in acceleration (hip 0.48, knee 0.37, ankle 0.74 J/kg) and negative in deceleration (hip -0.73, knee -0.65, ankle -0.54 J/kg), and net work differed between tasks at every joint (p < 0.001). Positive work was greater in acceleration at the hip and ankle (p < 0.001) but not at the knee (p = 0.014, above the 0.01 threshold), and negative work was greater in deceleration at all three joints (p < 0.001). The peak hip extension moment was -1.88 N m/kg in acceleration and -4.97 N m/kg in deceleration, the peak knee extension moment was -1.66 and -2.30 N m/kg, and the peak ankle plantarflexion moment was larger in acceleration (-2.86 versus -1.76 N m/kg).
paper.limitations: Twenty recreationally active adults in a laboratory, with the authors noting that sprint and deceleration mechanics may differ in elite or previously injured athletes. No sex-specific analysis was possible, and deceleration strategies varied across participants. Joint angles from skin markers are subject to soft-tissue artefact, and the laboratory setting differs from field play; forward velocity at foot strike differed by 5% between tasks, and the authors report that a covariate-adjusted model did not change any conclusion. The design is cross-sectional, so injury mechanisms in the discussion are inferences. One co-author holds interests in Vald Performance, which supplied the timing gates.
paper.practicalImplications: Deceleration placed larger negative work and peak extension demands on the knee and hip than acceleration did, so eccentric knee and hip extensor strength may be relevant to deceleration performance, as the authors propose. The mechanics should not be assumed to indicate injury risk, because injury was not measured. Findings from recreational adults should be checked against athletes before they inform training prescription.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Maximal acceleration depended mainly on ankle plantarflexor and hip extensor work, while deceleration depended on knee and hip extensor work. These are mechanical descriptions in recreational adults rather than performance outcomes, so they do not show that training these muscles improves sprint or change-of-direction performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not include injured athletes or return to sport. The authors suggest that the high eccentric hip and knee demands of deceleration may relate to hamstring, groin and ACL injury mechanisms, but they state that injury risk was beyond the scope of the study, so this paper cannot inform return-to-play loading or clearance.

records.sourceFile: Lower body blood flow restriction training may induce remote muscle strength adaptations in%c2%a0an%c2%a0active unrestricted arm.pdf

paper.citation: May AK, Russell AP, Warmington SA. Lower body blood flow restriction training may induce remote muscle strength adaptations in an active unrestricted arm. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2018.
paper.abstract: Twenty-four recreationally active young men were randomised to 8 weeks of leg resistance training with or without blood flow restriction, while both groups trained the dominant arm with bicep curls. The BFR group gained more elbow flexion 1-RM in the trained arm than the untrained arm and the controls' trained arm, and more knee extension 1-RM than controls. Muscle cross-sectional area changes did not differ between groups, and the authors attribute the remote strength effect mainly to neuromuscular adaptation.
paper.tldr: Adding light-load blood flow restriction to leg training was associated with a larger strength gain in a concurrently trained arm than arm training alone in 24 young men. Muscle size did not differ between groups, and the study did not test athletes, injured people or women.
paper.methods: Randomized two-group trial of 24 recreationally active young men (BFR group n = 12; non-BFR control n = 12) over 8 weeks, with 20 sessions three times per week. The dominant arm performed three sets of 10 unilateral bicep curls at 50% 1-RM, and both groups performed knee extension and flexion at 30% 1-RM. The BFR group used individually set cuff pressure at 60% limb occlusion pressure during leg exercise. Strength was measured by 1-RM in both arms and legs, and muscle cross-sectional area by peripheral quantitative CT at one leg site (25% femur length) and at 50% humerus length. Results are mean +/- SEM with mixed-model ANOVA and ANCOVA, with significance at p < 0.05.
paper.findings: Elbow flexion 1-RM increased by 2.5 +/- 0.4 kg in the BFR group's trained arm, compared with 0.8 +/- 0.4 kg in its untrained arm and 0.6 +/- 0.3 kg in the controls' trained arm (p < 0.05 for both comparisons). Knee extension 1-RM rose 16.3 +/- 1.3 kg in the BFR group and 8.3 +/- 1.6 kg in controls (p < 0.01). Knee flexion 1-RM and leg muscle cross-sectional area increased similarly in both groups, and trained-arm cross-sectional area did not differ between groups. The untrained arm did not change significantly in cross-sectional area.
paper.limitations: Only 12 men per group, all young and recreationally active, and the authors caution against generalising to women or clinical populations. Muscle size was measured at one leg site and by pQCT, so the null hypertrophy result is limited, and the authors suggest MRI at several sites in future work. The trained arm was always the dominant arm, and baseline elbow flexion strength was higher in the controls' trained arm than their untrained arm (p < 0.001). The abstract describes 7 weeks of training while the methods describe 20 sessions with post-testing in week 8. Participants gripped the machine handles during leg exercise, which the authors suggest may have recruited arm muscles more in the BFR group but judge to be negligible, and sitting on the cuffs during knee flexion may have reduced the restriction stimulus. The conclusion that the effect is neuromuscular rests partly on the null size result.
paper.practicalImplications: In this study, adding BFR to leg training produced a larger elbow flexion strength gain in a concurrently trained arm than arm training alone. The untrained arm did not differ from controls, and the authors suggest that a local mechanical stimulus in the arm may be needed, so leg BFR should not be expected to strengthen an arm that is not trained. The evidence rests on one small trial, so it should be treated as a hypothesis for athletes rather than a protocol.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: In recreationally active young men, leg BFR training combined with arm training increased trained-arm elbow flexion strength more than arm training alone over 8 weeks, which may be relevant to programmes that develop an arm alongside lower-body work. The study did not test athletes or sport performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not include injured people or return-to-sport outcomes. The authors suggest the approach may help people with localised movement disorders in early rehabilitation, but clinical groups were not tested, so the paper cannot guide load, cuff pressure or clearance in rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: Lowest perceived exertion in the late morning due to effects of the endogenous circadian system.pdf

paper.citation: Thosar SS, Herzig MX, Roberts SA, Berman AM, Clemons NA, McHill AW, et al. Lowest perceived exertion in the late morning due to effects of the endogenous circadian system. Br J Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: This research letter describes a forced desynchrony study of ten healthy adults that tested whether rate of perceived exertion (RPE) changes with the internal circadian clock when workload and behaviour are held constant. RPE was lowest in the late morning and highest during the biological night for the same mild-intensity cycling.
paper.tldr: In healthy adults, the same mild cycling workload felt least demanding in the late morning and most demanding in the biological night, independent of sleep, activity and meal timing. The study did not include athletes or high-intensity work.
paper.methods: Ten healthy adults (six female, mean age 52 years) went through a forced desynchrony protocol in dim light with repeated 5 hour 20 minute behavioural cycles. About one hour after each sleep episode they cycled for 15 minutes at 50% predicted maximal heart rate, and Borg RPE was recorded at 3, 8 and 13 minutes. RPE was Z-scored within each participant, grouped into 60 degree circadian phase bins and compared with repeated measures ANOVA, with circadian phase set from dim light melatonin onset.
paper.findings: The circadian system significantly affected RPE for the same workload, with the lowest RPE at circadian phase 210 degrees (about 10:45 AM) and the highest at 90 degrees (about 3:45 AM). The size of the circadian variation was about 1 Z-score unit (1 SD).
paper.limitations: The sample was small (n = 10) and was not made up of athletes. Only mild-intensity cycling was tested, and RPE was rated at only three time points within each bout. The authors' suggestion about athletes performing high-intensity exercise is untested in this study, and the text does not report a p-value.
paper.practicalImplications: Under controlled, mild cycling in healthy middle-aged adults, RPE for the same workload varied with circadian phase. Staff who compare RPE across sessions held at very different times of day may want to record session time, but the study did not test athletes or normal daytime training windows. It does not justify changing athlete session times or using light exposure to shift circadian timing.
paper.athleteDev: This study cannot be used to set athlete session times. It suggests that RPE for a fixed workload may be lower in the late morning, so RPE comparisons across different times of day should be interpreted with that in mind.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It included no injured participants and no return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Many pieces to the Puzzle - A new holistic workload approach to designing practice in sports.pdf

paper.citation: Champion L, Middleton K, MacMahon C. Many Pieces to the Puzzle: A New Holistic Workload Approach to Designing Practice in Sports. Sports Medicine - Open. 2023;9:38.
paper.abstract: The paper argues that representative learning design should weigh how closely training matches competition (fidelity) against the cognitive and physical load it imposes. It proposes a total workload approach with four characteristics and five training categories, linked to the perception-action cycle.
paper.tldr: The authors argue that highly match-like training should aid transfer but also adds cognitive and physical load that can contribute to fatigue, injury or burnout. They propose planning fidelity and load together across a week or cycle, alternating high and low demand.
paper.methods: Narrative conceptual review drawing on representative learning design, ecological dynamics and meshed control theory, with examples mainly from team sport. The paper describes no search strategy, database or appraisal method, and collects no data.
paper.findings: The authors state that representative training improves transfer but can add substantial cognitive and physical load, and that existing models do not quantify cognitive demand in training. They propose four characteristics and five training categories, and show a hypothetical seven-day microcycle in which cognitive and physical emphasis alternate. No validation or athlete outcome data are reported.
paper.limitations: The framework has no empirical testing, and the authors note that it does not dictate how fidelity or load should be measured. They also state that EEG, MEG and pupillometry can estimate cognitive workload but restrict movement, so practical measurement remains unresolved.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan match-like training together with its recovery demands rather than by volume alone, and consider cognitive as well as physical load when programming. The authors suggest that, until better measures exist, simpler tools such as session RPE and subjective fidelity ratings may be used, especially at sub-elite levels.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the framework to balance match-like drills against their load across a microcycle, treating cognitive demand as a planning variable. The framework is not validated and should be trialled before it changes programming.
paper.rtp: The paper does not address rehabilitation or return to sport. Its overload concerns apply to healthy training design, and it gives no return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Mechanisms of mechanical overload-induced skeletal muscle hypertrophy - Current understanding and future directions.pdf

paper.citation: Roberts MD, McCarthy JJ, Hornberger TA, Phillips SM, Mackey AL, Nader GA, et al. Mechanisms of mechanical overload-induced skeletal muscle hypertrophy: current understanding and future directions. Physiol Rev. 2023;103:2679-2757.
paper.abstract: The review traces the history of hypertrophy research and summarises the mechanisms linked to overload-induced muscle growth. It highlights mTORC1 signalling, translational capacity, satellite cells and myonuclear accretion, and it proposes directions for future research.
paper.tldr: Resistance training increases muscle mass through a few well-supported mechanisms, including mTORC1 signalling, ribosome biogenesis and satellite cell activity. Many other proposed mechanisms remain unproven, so the mechanistic picture is incomplete.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no search strategy reported. The authors present a historical account, a summary of mechanisms with a table of current role and knowledge gaps for each, and a discussion of methodological issues in hypertrophy research.
paper.findings: The authors identify enhanced mTORC1 signalling, expansion of translational capacity through ribosome biogenesis, and satellite cell-mediated myonuclear accretion as the mechanisms with the most support. They present other candidates (mTORC1-independent signalling, genetic variants, DNA methylation, proteolysis, myostatin, extracellular matrix remodelling, angiogenesis, microRNAs and prostaglandin signalling) as contributors with mixed or incomplete evidence, and rate testosterone signalling, endogenous beta-adrenergic signalling, angiotensin II, the muscle circadian clock and microtubule networks as not well elucidated. They also note that preliminary human data suggest individuals may differ in how they hypertrophy, with some gaining mainly through fascicle length and others through fibre cross-sectional area.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe a search or appraisal method, and the authors' own table marks several mechanisms as not well elucidated or as possibly only coinciding with hypertrophy. Much of the mechanistic evidence comes from rodent models, including the synergist ablation model that the authors say does not resemble progressive resistance training, and the review covers sex, race and ageing only briefly. Some authors report industry funding, including dairy industry grants.
paper.practicalImplications: Resistance training programmes should be built on progressive mechanical overload, which the authors describe as the stimulus that best achieves hypertrophy. The review reports that transient post-exercise rises in circulating hormones do not correlate with hypertrophy, and that high-dose ibuprofen (1,200 mg/day) and cold-water immersion may blunt hypertrophy-related responses, although findings are mixed and appear age dependent. Individual molecular mechanisms should not be treated as training targets.
paper.athleteDev: Use the review to explain why progressive overload is the core of hypertrophy work for athletes, while treating individual mechanisms as research questions rather than training targets. Individual responses may differ, so track each athlete's own change over time.
paper.rtp: The review concerns hypertrophy mechanisms during loading in healthy and general adult populations and does not address rehabilitation after injury, return-to-sport loading or tissue healing. It should not be used to set return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Mental fatigue impairs sprint and jump performance in team sport athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Staiano W, Salazar Bonet LR, Romagnoli M, Ring C. Mental Fatigue Impairs Repeated Sprint and Jump Performance in Team Sport Athletes. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2023.
paper.abstract: In 18 male team-sport players, a 30-minute Stroop task increased mental fatigue and rating of perceived exertion compared with a documentary. Mental fatigue impaired directional repeated sprint performance and repeated jump performance, but not linear sprinting, peak performance or a single countermovement jump.
paper.tldr: A 30-minute Stroop task made team-sport players slower and less consistent in directional repeated sprints and repeated jumps. Linear sprints and single jumps were not affected, and the effect was linked to higher perceived effort rather than blood lactate or heart rate.
paper.methods: Eighteen male amateur basketball, handball and football players completed a familiarization session and then two counterbalanced conditions at least 10 days apart: a 30-minute Stroop task or a documentary. Afterwards they completed 12 maximal 20-m sprints (10 m linear plus 10 m directional), 12 maximal repeated countermovement jumps and a countermovement jump test, with mental fatigue, psychomotor vigilance, RPE, heart rate and lactate measured.
paper.findings: Mean directional sprint time was longer after the Stroop task (P = 0.032) and sprint decrement was greater (P = 0.027). In the repeated jump test, mean jump height was lower (P = 0.009, d = 0.60) and decrement greater (P = 0.034) after the Stroop task. Peak sprint time, peak jump height, countermovement jump height, heart rate and lactate did not differ, while RPE was higher and psychomotor vigilance reaction time was slower than control (P = 0.002).
paper.limitations: The authors note the lack of biomechanical measures of postural control, so their proposed mechanism is speculative. The sample was 18 amateur men at one performance level (no women could be tested), and the study tested a single 30-minute Stroop protocol against a documentary control.
paper.practicalImplications: Demanding cognitive work before a session may reduce the quality of repeated directional sprints and repeated jumps, and the authors advise coaches in sports with repeated sprinting and jumping to plan strategies to limit mental fatigue. They suggest power naps, self-talk, caffeine and brain endurance training, but this study tested none of them.
paper.athleteDev: Mentally fatiguing work before a session may reduce the quality of directional repeated sprints and repeated jumps in team-sport athletes, so the timing of cognitive load matters. Linear sprinting and single jumps were not affected in this study.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy players and did not measure injury or return-to-play readiness, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Mental fatigue impairs tackling technique in amateur rugby union players.pdf

paper.citation: Davidow D, Smith M, Ross T, James GL, Paul L, Lambert M, et al. Mental Fatigue Impairs Tackling Technique in Amateur Rugby Union Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2023.
paper.abstract: Twenty male amateur rugby union players tackled a simulator on both shoulders in a control condition and after a 30-minute Stroop task. Tackling proficiency was lower after the Stroop task, mainly on the non-dominant shoulder, with small effect sizes.
paper.tldr: Mental fatigue reduced the technical quality of tackles, most clearly on the non-dominant shoulder. The effects were small, and the study used a tackle simulator rather than live tackles.
paper.methods: Twenty players completed a four-set tackle protocol (three tackles per shoulder per set) on a tackle contact simulator at two counterbalanced visits at least 72 hours apart. One visit included passive reading and the other a 30-minute Stroop task with 5-minute top-ups after sets 1 and 2. Each tackle was video-scored by one assessor against 11 technical criteria, and mental fatigue, physical fatigue, RPE and mental effort were rated on visual analogue scales.
paper.findings: Across both shoulders, tackle proficiency was lower in the Stroop condition at set 2 (6.91 vs 7.30 AU, P = 0.009) and set 3 (6.88 vs 7.34 AU, P = 0.002). On the non-dominant shoulder the difference was significant at set 2 (P = 0.047) and set 3 (6.61 vs 7.14 AU, P = 0.007), while the dominant shoulder showed no between-condition difference. Explosiveness on contact was the component most impaired on both shoulders, and mental fatigue and physical fatigue ratings were higher after the Stroop task.
paper.limitations: Baseline tackle proficiency was higher in the Stroop condition (7.47 vs 7.08 AU, P = 0.009), which may affect the between-condition comparison. The authors note the simulator has only moderate ecological validity, the Stroop task's ecological validity has been questioned, and effects at junior, elite or female levels are unknown.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors recommend including a mental fatigue component in tackle training, for example by asking players to tackle while performing a demanding cognitive task. This study did not test that training approach, so its benefit is untested.
paper.athleteDev: Mentally fatiguing demands may reduce the explosive, on-contact quality of tackles, especially on the non-dominant shoulder, so technical training under cognitive load may be worth trying. The effect came from one 30-minute Stroop protocol in a simulator, so it should be treated as a hypothesis for training design.
paper.rtp: The study did not measure injury, live tackling or return-to-play readiness, so it cannot decide when a player can return to contact. Its link to tackle injury risk comes from the literature the authors cite, not from a finding of this trial.

records.sourceFile: Multiscale hamstring muscle adaptations following 9 weeks of eccentric training.pdf

paper.citation: Andrews MH, Anoosha Pai S, Gurchiek RD, Pincheira PA, Chaudhari AS, Hodges PW, et al. Multiscale hamstring muscle adaptations following 9 weeks of eccentric training. Journal of Sport and Health Science. 2024.
paper.abstract: Twelve recreationally active adults completed 9 weeks of Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) training followed by 3 weeks of detraining. Biceps femoris long-head fascicle length increased (19% central, 33% distal) and serial sarcomere number increased (25% central, 49% distal), with muscle volume (8%) and knee flexion strength (40%) also rising. Fascicle length partly reverted after detraining.
paper.tldr: Nine weeks of Nordic hamstring training lengthened hamstring fascicles and increased muscle volume and eccentric strength in a small group of recreationally active adults. The sarcomere-level results are indirect, and the study does not show injury protection.
paper.methods: Longitudinal single-group design with 3 NHE sessions a week for 9 weeks, then 3 weeks of detraining, and no control group. Fascicle length was measured with 3D freehand ultrasound, sarcomere length with second harmonic generation microendoscopy, muscle volume with MRI, and eccentric knee flexor torque with load cells on the ankle straps.
paper.findings: Fascicle length increased significantly over training, with a larger change distally, and serial sarcomere number increased significantly (per the abstract, 25% central and 49% distal). Sarcomere length did not change significantly (p = 0.083). Muscle volume and eccentric strength increased, strength stayed above baseline after detraining, and fascicle length fell by 12% (central) and 16% (distal) during detraining.
paper.limitations: Twelve participants, no control group, and sarcomere measurements were sparse, so the detraining sarcomere data were excluded from the statistics. Serial sarcomere number is a calculated value, and the abstract's statement that sarcomeres were added in series rests on that calculation and on a sarcomere length change that was not significant.
paper.practicalImplications: A 9-week NHE programme lengthened biceps femoris fascicles and increased strength in recreationally active adults, so the exercise is a reasonable option for building hamstring architecture. Fascicle gains partly reversed within 3 weeks of detraining and strength fell (p = 0.006) while staying above baseline, so the stimulus needs to be maintained if the changes are to last.
paper.athleteDev: Shows that 9 weeks of NHE lengthened biceps femoris fascicles and increased muscle volume and eccentric strength in recreationally active adults. It does not test sprint or sport performance.
paper.rtp: Can inform that eccentric hamstring training changes muscle architecture and strength over weeks, but it cannot clear anyone to return to sport or estimate injury risk. It included no injured participants and no return-to-sport outcome.

records.sourceFile: Muscle forces and fascicle behavior during three hamstring exercises.pdf

paper.citation: Van Hooren B, Vanwanseele B, van Rossom S, Teratsias P, Willems P, Drost M, et al. Muscle forces and fascicle behavior during three hamstring exercises. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2022.
paper.abstract: Ten male athletes performed the Nordic hamstring curl, single-leg Roman chair hold and single-leg deadlift while kinematics, ground reaction forces, surface EMG and biceps femoris long-head fascicle length were recorded. The Nordic curl produced the highest peak hamstring forces and the greatest fascicle excursion, and the authors suggest it may be the most effective of the three for increasing fascicle length.
paper.tldr: Across three popular hamstring exercises, the Nordic curl produced the highest peak hamstring forces and the largest fascicle lengthening in a single session. These acute mechanics do not show which exercise produces the best long-term change.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional laboratory study with 10 male athletes performing the three exercises in random order in one session. Full-body 3D motion capture, force plates, surface EMG and B-mode ultrasound of the biceps femoris long head were used, and muscle forces were estimated with inverse dynamics and optimisation in a modified OpenSim model.
paper.findings: Fascicle excursion over the whole exercise was highest in the Nordic curl, significantly greater than in the deadlift. Mean fascicle length was highest in the deadlift, then the Roman chair, then the Nordic curl. Peak forces were higher in the Nordic curl than in both other exercises for the biceps femoris short head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus, and higher than the deadlift for the biceps femoris long head.
paper.limitations: One session, 10 men, and forces estimated by a model rather than measured. Fascicle lengthening velocity during the Nordic curl had poor reliability (ICC 0.42), and the study did not measure training adaptations. The abstract says fascicle lengthening was higher in the Nordic curl than in both other exercises, but Table 1 shows whole-exercise excursion was significantly greater only versus the deadlift (Nordic vs Roman chair 12.6 mm, 95% CI -1.6 to 26.7). The authors' suggestions about which exercise builds which muscle are inferences from acute mechanics rather than results of training.
paper.practicalImplications: The Nordic curl produced significantly more acute fascicle excursion than the deadlift and higher peak forces in three hamstring muscles than both other exercises, while mean eccentric forces were mostly similar between the Nordic curl and Roman chair. This is a useful mechanical comparison when selecting exercises. Training studies are needed before choosing an exercise for a specific adaptation.
paper.athleteDev: Shows how three hamstring exercises differ acutely in fascicle lengthening and hamstring force, which may help exercise selection. It does not measure sprint or sport performance, so the performance link is untested.
paper.rtp: Can inform that the Nordic curl and Roman chair load the hamstrings differently from the deadlift, but cannot show that any exercise reduces re-injury or is safe for return to sport. No injured athletes were included.

records.sourceFile: Muscle morphological changes and enhanced sprint running performance - A 1-year observational study of well-trained sprinters.pdf

paper.citation: Kawama R, Takahashi K, Tozawa H, Obata T, Fuji N, Arai A, et al. Muscle morphological changes and enhanced sprint running performance: a 1-year observational study of well-trained sprinters. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024.
paper.abstract: Measured 100 m and split sprint velocities and MRI muscle volumes in 23 male collegiate athletes before and after one year of their own daily training. Sprint velocity increased, and relative volumes of the tensor fasciae latae, sartorius, biceps femoris long and short heads, semitendinosus and iliacus increased. Among the hypertrophied muscles, only the change in semitendinosus volume correlated with the change in 50-60 m velocity.
paper.tldr: Over one year of ordinary daily training, collegiate athletes' sprint speed rose along with several thigh muscles, and only semitendinosus growth tracked the gain in top-end speed. This is an association in one group without a control, not a tested training prescription.
paper.methods: Longitudinal observational study without intervention. Twenty-three male collegiate athletes had 100 m sprint splits from timing gates and high-speed video, and T1-weighted MRI of 14 trunk and thigh muscles, before and after one year of daily training. Changes were tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and changes in muscle volume were correlated with changes in sprint velocity with Spearman correlations and a false discovery rate correction.
paper.findings: The 100 m time improved from a median of 11.69 s to 11.49 s (p < 0.001), and 50-60 m velocity rose from 9.52 to 9.71 m/s (p = 0.018). Relative volumes increased for the TFL, sartorius, biceps femoris long and short heads, semitendinosus and iliacus, and decreased for the rectus femoris. The change in relative semitendinosus volume correlated with the change in 50-60 m velocity (rho = 0.591, p = 0.018), and no other muscle-speed correlation was significant.
paper.limitations: No control group, two sprint tests only, and wind was higher at the second test, so the conditions were not comparable. The false discovery rate correction is described for the correlations, while the muscle-volume comparisons across 14 muscles are reported without it, and the semitendinosus link did not appear in any spatiotemporal sprint variable, leaving the mechanism unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Training that combined sprint, jump and resistance work was followed by faster speed and larger size in several thigh muscles, so staff can monitor muscle size and split times together over a season. The semitendinosus link should be treated as a hypothesis to test, not a rule for choosing exercises.
paper.athleteDev: Shows that a year of ordinary sprint, jump and resistance training was followed by faster 100 m and 50-60 m speed and larger thigh muscles in collegiate athletes. The semitendinosus association is a lead for testing, not a prescription.
paper.rtp: Not designed for return to sport: the athletes were healthy by inclusion and no injured athletes were studied. It cannot be used to judge when an athlete is ready to return to sprinting after injury.

records.sourceFile: Narrative Review - The role of circadian rhythm on sports performance, hormonal regulation, immune system function, and injury prevention in ath.pdf

paper.citation: Nobari H, Azarian S, Saedmocheshi S, Valdés-Badilla P, García Calvo T. Narrative review: The role of circadian rhythm on sports performance, hormonal regulation, immune system function, and injury prevention in athletes. Heliyon. 2023;9:e19636.
paper.abstract: Review of circadian rhythm (CR) and its links to sports performance, endocrine homeostasis, sex differences and immune function in athletes. The authors searched PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science for English-language peer-reviewed studies to July 2023. They report that performance measures tend to peak in the afternoon, that CR can be shifted by light, exercise and feeding, and that sleep loss and time of day interact to affect performance, a point drawn from cited studies rather than new data.
paper.tldr: A review arguing that time of day affects athletic performance, hormones, immune function and recovery, and that sleep and diet can shift circadian timing. Much of the evidence is mechanistic, animal-based or from non-athletes, so the practical recommendations are suggestions rather than tested protocols.
paper.methods: The authors call this a narrative review, but it describes a database search, so the library codes it as a systematic review by precedent. PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science (core collection) were searched with the terms circadian rhythm, sports performance, hormonal regulation, immune system and injury prevention, limited to English, peer-reviewed studies published up to July 2023 that examined CR in athletes, and the authors say the search followed PRISMA. No counts of records screened, quality appraisal or pooled analysis are reported, and synthesis was narrative.
paper.findings: The review states that many performance measures peak in the afternoon or early evening, with anaerobic performance usually described as peaking in the evening, although one passage places muscle power and anaerobic capacity peaks in the early morning, and it calls evidence for aerobic performance inconsistent. It cites a study of 11 endurance runners during Ramadan in which glucose peaked around 20:00 and 04:00, and a study in which lactate after the Wingate test was higher in the evening than the morning. It reports that lack of sleep seems to affect evening performance more than morning performance, and it cites one study in which a 30-minute afternoon nap after a short night improved running performance. For injury, the text gives inconsistent figures for adolescent athletes sleeping under 8 hours (1.7 times more injuries in one section, OR 2.1 in another), and a Swedish study reporting OR 0.39 for more than 8 hours.
paper.limitations: The authors say the review lacks signaling-pathway and molecular evidence, has limited evidence on training models, and relies on mechanistic and rodent studies for several claims. Study selection, screening and quality appraisal are not described in enough detail to reproduce the search. The Discussion's injury figures conflict (1.7 times vs OR 2.1), the review places muscle power and anaerobic capacity peaks in both the evening and the early morning, and the abstract's claim that the sleep-by-time-of-day interaction was 'established in this study' is unsupported because the paper contains no original data.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use the review to prompt timing questions, for example scheduling key high-intensity or power sessions in the afternoon where feasible and checking athletes' sleep before early training or travel. Claims about specific foods, supplements and melatonin doses should not be adopted without checking the primary studies and the athlete's medical and anti-doping status.
paper.athleteDev: The review supports considering time of day and individual chronotype when scheduling sessions, testing and competition. It gives conflicting timing for power and anaerobic peaks, and its performance claims are largely drawn from short-term or mechanistic studies, so they should be tested in the local squad before they change training plans.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return-to-sport testing or rehabilitation timing. Its injury and sleep associations come from observational adolescent data with conflicting figures, so they should not be used to decide when an injured athlete can return to play.

records.sourceFile: Neuromechanics of the rate of force development.pdf

paper.citation: Del Vecchio A. Neuromechanics of the Rate of Force Development. Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews. 2023;51(1):34-42.
paper.abstract: A review of how neural drive and muscle properties determine the maximal rate of force development (RFD) in healthy individuals. The author hypothesizes that differences between people are mainly due to how fast motor units are recruited, and supports this with previously published motor unit recordings from 20 men, computer simulations, and a reanalysis of spike frequency adaptation in 242 motor neurons.
paper.tldr: Differences between people in how quickly they develop force appear to be driven mainly by how fast motor units are recruited. Early motor unit discharge rate also contributes, while muscle properties play a smaller part in this account.
paper.methods: A review article with new analyses of previously published data. The author reports motor unit discharge in 20 men, a reanalysis of spike frequency adaptation across 242 motor neurons from 20 subjects, computer simulations using data from 25 people, and force data from three muscle groups. No literature search method is described.
paper.findings: The fastest of 20 men reached a peak motor unit discharge rate of about 200 Hz, compared with about 100 Hz in the slowest, and had about twice the recruitment rate. In simulations, varying the recruitment interval had a more than fourfold greater effect on RFD than varying initial discharge rate, and the author describes a faster nervous system as about six times more efficient than a faster muscle. After 4 weeks of high-force training, maximal force increased but RFD and early (first 50 ms) force impulse did not change, which the author links to unchanged recruitment interval and initial discharge rate.
paper.limitations: Most motor unit data come from tibialis anterior, and the author notes that other muscles could differ. The recruitment-rate measure depends on how many motor units are detected, which the author acknowledges. Subject characteristics are given only by reference to earlier studies, and the author notes that muscle properties may dominate after injury or disuse.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff analysing rapid force tests could treat the force-time curve as a continuous signal, as the author recommends, rather than relying only on fixed time windows, which he describes as arbitrary thresholds. The author reports that early and late rapid force are strongly related, so early and late phases should not be read as purely neural or purely muscular.
paper.athleteDev: The modelled 4-week heavy strength training study raised maximal force without changing RFD, so maximal strength gains alone may not improve rapid force in this account. These findings come from healthy adults, mostly one muscle, and simulations, so they should not alone be used to design athlete RFD training.
paper.rtp: The paper does not address return to sport, injury or rehabilitation. It notes that some individuals may have weaker muscle after injury, disuse or other factors, but it provides no return-to-play criteria and should not be used for return-to-play decisions.
